title: PostgreSQL Connection Refused
symptoms: psycopg2.OperationalError: could not connect to server
Service failing to connect to PostgreSQL after retries
Order processing or core service halted
root_causes: PostgreSQL process crashed or was OOM-killed
Database migration in recent deployment caused lock or crash
Max connections limit reached (check max_connections and pg_stat_activity)
Firewall rule change blocking port 5432
pgbouncer connection pool exhausted
resolution_steps: 1. SSH into db-prod-01 and check PostgreSQL process: `systemctl status postgresql`
2. Check PostgreSQL logs: `tail -n 100 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql.log`
3. If process is down, restart: `systemctl restart postgresql`
4. Check active connections: `SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;`
5. If max connections exceeded, kill idle connections: `SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle' AND query_start < NOW() - INTERVAL '5 minutes';`
6. Check if recent migration caused table locks: `SELECT * FROM pg_locks WHERE granted = false;`
7. If deployment-related, consider rollback of order-service to previous version
8. Verify firewall rules: `iptables -L | grep 5432`
prevention: Add connection pool monitoring alerts
Run migrations in separate pipeline before deploying application
Configure PostgreSQL HA with automatic failover (Patroni or RDS Multi-AZ)
Set connection timeout and retry with exponential backoff in application
escalation: If DB cannot be restarted within 10 minutes, page DBA on-call. If data loss suspected, escalate to engineering lead immediately.

title: Service OOM Kill / Memory Exhaustion
root_causes: Memory leak in recent code deployment
Kubernetes memory limit set too low for current load
Unbounded cache growing without eviction policy
Large batch job consuming excessive memory
N+1 query loading too much data into memory
resolution_steps: 1. Confirm OOM kill: `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> | grep -A5 'Last State'`
2. Check current memory limits: `kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o yaml | grep -A4 resources`
3. Temporary fix — increase memory limit: `kubectl set resources deployment <name> --limits=memory=2Gi`
4. Check for memory leak — review heap dumps or profiler output from the crashing instance
5. Identify the largest memory consumers in the recent deployment diff
6. If batch job is the cause, throttle or reschedule to off-peak hours
7. Add memory usage alerts at 80% threshold
prevention: Set memory requests and limits on all pods
Add JVM heap size flags (-Xmx) for Java services
Implement cache size limits with LRU eviction
Load test before deploying services with significant logic changes
escalation: If service cannot stabilize after limit increase, escalate to owning team. If production data pipeline is affected, page data engineering lead.

title: API Gateway 502 Bad Gateway
symptoms: 502 Bad Gateway responses from API gateway
All requests failing at gateway layer
Health checks failing for upstream service
root_causes: Upstream service is down or not responding
Upstream service taking longer than gateway timeout
SSL certificate expired on upstream service
Upstream service returning invalid HTTP response
Load balancer has no healthy backend instances
resolution_steps: 1. Check gateway logs for specific upstream error: `kubectl logs -n gateway <gateway-pod>`
2. Test upstream service directly: `curl -v http://<upstream-service>:<port>/health`
3. Check upstream service pod status: `kubectl get pods -n <namespace>`
4. If upstream is down, restart it: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/<upstream-service>`
5. Check gateway timeout configuration — increase if upstream is slow
6. Verify SSL certificates: `openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 | grep 'notAfter'`
7. Check load balancer target group health in AWS console
prevention: Set up upstream health check alerts
Configure circuit breaker pattern on gateway
Monitor SSL certificate expiry with 30-day advance alerts
Implement retry logic with exponential backoff at gateway level
escalation: If upstream cannot be restored within 15 minutes, escalate to owning team and consider enabling maintenance page.

title: Redis Cache Connection Failure
root_causes: Redis instance crashed or was restarted
Redis memory limit reached causing eviction storm
Network partition between application and Redis
Redis connection pool exhausted
Incorrect Redis URL or credentials after config change
resolution_steps: 1. Check Redis status: `redis-cli -h <redis-host> ping`
2. Check Redis logs: `tail -n 50 /var/log/redis/redis-server.log`
3. Check memory usage: `redis-cli info memory | grep used_memory_human`
4. If memory full, flush expired keys: `redis-cli --scan --pattern '*' | xargs redis-cli unlink`
5. Restart Redis if crashed: `systemctl restart redis`
6. Verify application Redis URL in config matches actual Redis endpoint
7. Check connection pool settings — reduce max connections if pool exhausted
8. Confirm application can operate in degraded mode without cache
prevention: Set Redis maxmemory-policy to allkeys-lru
Monitor Redis memory usage with alert at 80%
Implement graceful cache fallback in application code
Use Redis Sentinel or Cluster for high availability
escalation: Redis failure alone is usually not critical if application has cache fallback. Escalate if response times exceed SLA thresholds.

title: Kubernetes Pod CrashLoopBackOff
symptoms: Exit code 1 or non-zero exit codes
root_causes: Application startup error due to missing environment variable
Failed database migration on startup
Incorrect container image or image pull failure
Readiness probe misconfigured causing premature kill
Application crash on startup due to code bug in new deployment
resolution_steps: 1. Check pod events: `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>`
2. Check pod logs from previous crashed instance: `kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous`
3. Check for missing environment variables in pod spec
4. Verify image exists and is pullable: `kubectl describe pod | grep Image`
5. If new deployment, rollback immediately: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>`
6. Check if init containers are failing: `kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <init-container-name>`
7. Temporarily increase backoff time to read logs before next restart: increase terminationGracePeriodSeconds
prevention: Run smoke tests in staging before production deployment
Validate all required environment variables are set in deployment manifests
Use readiness and liveness probes correctly
Implement canary deployments to catch issues before full rollout
escalation: If rollback does not resolve within 2 restart cycles, escalate to owning team. If all pods in deployment are crashing, declare incident immediately.

title: High Database Query Latency / Slow Queries
root_causes: Missing index on frequently queried column
N+1 query pattern introduced in recent deployment
Table lock contention from long-running transaction
Autovacuum not running causing bloat
Sudden spike in traffic overwhelming query planner
resolution_steps: 1. Identify slow queries: `SELECT query, mean_exec_time, calls FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;`
2. Check for table locks: `SELECT * FROM pg_locks WHERE granted = false;`
3. Kill blocking queries: `SELECT pg_terminate_backend(<pid>);`
4. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on slow query to identify missing index
5. Add index if missing: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_<table>_<column> ON <table>(<column>);`
6. Check autovacuum status: `SELECT schemaname, tablename, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables;`
7. Manually trigger vacuum if needed: `VACUUM ANALYZE <table>;`
prevention: Set up slow query logging (log_min_duration_statement = 500ms)
Review EXPLAIN plans for new queries in code review
Monitor pg_stat_statements in dashboards
Run load tests against staging with production-size data
escalation: If latency cannot be reduced within 30 minutes and SLA is breached, escalate to DBA and engineering lead.

title: Message Queue Backlog / Consumer Lag
root_causes: Consumer service crashed or scaled down
Consumer throwing exceptions on specific message format
Consumer processing too slowly — throughput mismatch
Dead letter queue filling up with poison messages
Broker connectivity issue from consumer side
resolution_steps: 1. Check consumer group lag: `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group <group-name>`
2. Check consumer service logs for exceptions
3. If consumer is crashing on a specific message, identify and skip or move to DLQ
4. Scale up consumer instances: `kubectl scale deployment <consumer> --replicas=5`
5. Check for poison messages in DLQ and handle accordingly
6. Verify broker connectivity from consumer pods
7. If lag is extreme, consider resetting offset to current position to skip backlog (only if messages are non-critical)
prevention: Set up consumer lag alerts with threshold-based paging
Implement dead letter queue for all consumers
Add idempotency to consumer logic
Monitor consumer throughput vs producer throughput
escalation: If lag exceeds 1 hour of messages and consumer cannot recover, escalate to data engineering. If financial or order events are affected, escalate immediately.

title: SSL Certificate Expiry
root_causes: Certificate renewal not automated
Auto-renewal failed silently
Certificate renewed but not deployed
Wrong certificate deployed to server
resolution_steps: 1. Confirm expiry: `openssl s_client -connect <domain>:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates`
2. If using Let's Encrypt: `certbot renew --force-renewal`
3. If using AWS ACM: check certificate status in ACM console and trigger renewal
4. Redeploy updated certificate to load balancer or web server
5. Restart nginx/apache if certificate is file-based: `systemctl reload nginx`
6. Verify fix: `curl -vI https://<domain> 2>&1 | grep 'expire date'`
prevention: Set up certificate expiry monitoring with 30-day advance alerts
Automate certificate renewal with certbot or ACM
Test renewal process quarterly
Use wildcard certificates where possible to reduce surface area
escalation: SSL expiry is a P1 incident if it affects customer-facing endpoints. Escalate to security team and engineering lead immediately.

title: Deployment Rollback Procedure
symptoms: Error rate spike immediately after deployment
root_causes: Bug introduced in new code
Incompatible dependency version
Database migration incompatible with previous version
Configuration change causing unexpected behavior
resolution_steps: 1. Confirm the deployment is the cause by checking timing correlation
2. Kubernetes rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<service-name>`
3. Verify rollback status: `kubectl rollout status deployment/<service-name>`
4. Check that previous version is running: `kubectl get pods -l app=<service-name>`
5. If database migration was applied, assess whether it is reversible
6. Run down migration if safe: `alembic downgrade -1` or equivalent
7. Notify team of rollback via incident channel
8. Create post-deployment issue in tracker with reproduction steps
prevention: Use canary deployments — route 5% of traffic to new version before full rollout
Keep migrations backward compatible for at least one release cycle
Automate rollback trigger based on error rate threshold
Test rollback procedure in staging monthly
escalation: If rollback does not restore service within 10 minutes, escalate to engineering lead. If data was modified by the bad deployment, escalate to DBA.

title: Third-Party API Timeout / Degradation
symptoms: Timeout errors on external API calls
Increased response times for features using external service
Spike in circuit breaker open events
root_causes: Third-party service having an outage
Rate limit exceeded on third-party API
Network latency between our infra and their endpoint
Third-party API returning slow responses due to their internal issues
resolution_steps: 1. Check third-party status page for ongoing incidents
2. Check our rate limit usage: review API response headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining)
3. If rate limited, implement exponential backoff and reduce request frequency
4. Enable circuit breaker if not already open — fail fast rather than queuing
5. Switch to fallback behavior: cached data, degraded mode, or user-facing message
6. If critical, contact third-party support with your account ID and timestamps
7. Monitor their status page for resolution and re-enable once confirmed stable
prevention: Implement circuit breaker for all external API calls
Cache third-party responses where possible
Design graceful degradation for all third-party dependencies
Monitor third-party API latency as a separate metric
escalation: This is typically not escalatable internally — it is a third-party issue. Escalate to product team to communicate user impact and timeline.
resolution_time_estimate: Dependent on third-party — 30 minutes to several hours

title: Disk Space Exhaustion
symptoms: No space left on device error
Database unable to write new data
root_causes: Log files not being rotated or truncated
Database growing without archiving old data
Large temporary files from failed jobs
Docker image layers accumulating
Core dumps filling disk
resolution_steps: 1. Identify disk usage: `df -h` and `du -sh /* | sort -rh | head -20`
2. Find largest files: `find / -type f -size +500M 2>/dev/null`
3. Clear old logs: `journalctl --vacuum-size=500M` or truncate log files
4. Remove old Docker images: `docker image prune -a`
5. Remove core dumps: `find / -name 'core.*' -delete`
6. Archive or delete old database records if safe
7. Expand disk volume if immediate cleanup is insufficient
prevention: Set up log rotation with logrotate
Alert at 80% disk usage
Schedule regular cleanup jobs for temp files and old logs
Set Docker log driver with max-size limit
escalation: If disk cannot be freed quickly and database writes are failing, this is a P1. Escalate to infrastructure team to expand volume.

title: Authentication Service / JWT Token Failure
symptoms: invalid signature or expired token errors
root_causes: JWT signing secret rotated without updating all services
Clock skew between services causing token expiry mismatch
Auth service down causing token verification to fail
Wrong environment JWT secret deployed to production
Token expiry set too short in new deployment
resolution_steps: 1. Confirm scope — are all users affected or a subset?
2. Check auth service status: `kubectl get pods -n auth`
3. Verify JWT secret is consistent across all services using it
4. Check server time sync: `timedatectl status` on auth and API servers
5. If secret was rotated, redeploy all dependent services with new secret
6. If token expiry is the issue, adjust and redeploy auth service
7. Clear token cache if services cache validation results
prevention: Use centralized secret management (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault)
Automate secret rotation with zero-downtime strategy
Sync server clocks with NTP
Alert on 401 error rate spike
escalation: Auth failure affecting all users is a P1. Escalate to security team and engineering lead immediately. Do not attempt to bypass authentication as a fix.

title: Microservice Timeout / Cascading Failure
symptoms: Timeout errors propagating across multiple services
Thread pool exhaustion in upstream service
Response times growing across the system
root_causes: One slow downstream service causing upstream thread exhaustion
Missing timeout configuration causing requests to hang
Retry storms amplifying load on struggling service
Synchronous call chain with no circuit breaker
Database slowdown propagating through service mesh
resolution_steps: 1. Identify the origin service — find the first service to show degradation in traces
2. Check if one service is receiving disproportionate load
3. Enable circuit breaker on connections to the degraded service
4. Shed load — temporarily reject non-critical requests
5. Restart the struggling service if it is stuck
6. Review timeout configurations — ensure every HTTP call has a max timeout
7. Check for retry storms — confirm retries have backoff and jitter
prevention: Implement circuit breakers on all inter-service calls
Set explicit timeouts on all outbound HTTP calls
Use bulkhead pattern to isolate thread pools per dependency
Add distributed tracing to quickly identify origin of cascading failures
escalation: If more than 3 services are degraded simultaneously, declare a major incident. Page engineering lead and begin war room.

title: Data Pipeline Failure / ETL Job Error
symptoms: ETL job failing with transformation error
root_causes: Schema change in source table breaking transformation
Source data containing unexpected null or malformed values
Pipeline timing out due to increased data volume
Dependency service unavailable during job run
Insufficient memory or disk for transformation
resolution_steps: 1. Check job logs for the specific failure point and error message
2. Identify which transformation step failed
3. If schema change: update transformation to handle new schema
4. If null/malformed data: add validation and null handling to pipeline
5. If timeout: increase job timeout or break into smaller batches
6. Re-run failed job after fix: trigger manual run from scheduler
7. Verify output data matches expected row counts and freshness
prevention: Add schema validation at pipeline entry point
Set up data quality checks after each transformation step
Alert on job failure immediately rather than waiting for data freshness alert
Run pipelines with idempotency so reruns are safe
escalation: If pipeline has been failing for more than 2 hours and business reports are affected, escalate to data engineering lead and notify stakeholders.

title: CDN / Static Asset Serving Failure
symptoms: Frontend loading slowly or not at all
404 errors on CSS, JS, or image files
Assets loading from origin instead of edge
root_causes: CDN cache invalidation not completing after deployment
Origin S3 bucket permissions changed
CloudFront distribution misconfigured after update
Asset build failed silently — empty or corrupt files deployed
TTL too long serving stale assets after deployment
resolution_steps: 1. Check CDN error rate in CloudFront metrics or equivalent
2. Test asset URLs directly from origin: `curl -I https://<s3-origin>/<asset-path>`
3. If origin is fine, invalidate CDN cache: `aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id <id> --paths '/*'`
4. Check S3 bucket policy for public read access
5. Verify asset build output — check file sizes are non-zero
6. If distribution is misconfigured, check recent CloudFront configuration changes
7. As immediate mitigation, point traffic directly to origin while CDN is fixed
prevention: Automate cache invalidation as part of deployment pipeline
Add asset size validation to build step — fail build if output is empty
Monitor CDN error rates with alerts
Use versioned asset filenames to avoid cache issues on deploy
escalation: If frontend is completely non-functional and CDN cannot be fixed within 15 minutes, consider rolling back deployment or routing directly to origin.
